research.lens: Near Eastern archaeological chronology (Levant, Anatolia, Upper and Lower Mesopotamia, Zagros), from the Late Epipaleolithic Natufian through PPNA, PPNB/PPNC, Pottery Neolithic (Hassuna/Samarra/Halaf), Ubaid, and Late Chalcolithic/Uruk up to proto-cuneiform writing. For each period: dates, the social and economic features that define it, and where it fits G1-G6. Dates: cal BP minus 1950 gives cal BC. Many Ubaid, Halaf and Uruk ranges in the literature are conventional ceramic-phase dates, not modelled radiocarbon dates. These are flagged where relevant.

periods_or_stages.name: Early Natufian (Late Epipaleolithic), southern Levant
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 15,000/14,600-13,600 cal BP (about 12,650-11,650 cal BC). Shubayqa 1 occupied about 14,600-12,000 cal BP. Early Natufian at Ain Mallaha about 14,300 cal BP.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Foragers who stay in one place for long periods, before any farming. Hamlets of round, semi-subterranean houses with stone footings, 3-7 m across with a central hearth (Ain Mallaha/Eynan; Valla reconstructs about 12 round shelters). Heavy use of wild cereals and grinding tools, basalt vessels, burials under or near houses, a woman buried with a puppy (early dog). Art and personal ornaments. Bar-Yosef treats it as the 'threshold' to agriculture. Frequent rebuilding suggests people still moved often, so 'sedentary' is debated.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Start of G1 (村ができる). Villages and growing population appear before cultivation, so in the real sequence G1 comes before G2. No domestic plants or animals yet.
sources: Richter et al. 2017, Scientific Reports, Shubayqa 1 AMS dates (~14,600-11,500 cal BP for the Natufian) - https://xronos.ch/references/17778
Bar-Yosef, O. 1998. The Natufian culture in the Levant, threshold to the origins of agriculture. Evolutionary Anthropology 6:159-177 (citation confirmed; full text not read)

periods_or_stages.name: Late/Final Natufian
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 13,600-11,700/11,500 cal BP (about 11,650-9,550 cal BC). Overlaps the Younger Dryas cold phase (commonly about 12,900-11,700 cal BP; this figure not checked in this search).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Often described as a partial return to mobility under the Younger Dryas, but climate and cultural dates do not line up well, and gazelle isotopes suggest it was colder but not drier. Ritual feasting at burials: Hilazon Tachtit (about 12,000 cal BP) has a woman buried with more than 50 tortoises, plus wild cattle feasting remains. Munro & Grosman read this as feasting used to hold a growing community together.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Late G1. Ritual feasting holds a growing group together before any leaders exist. This is an early version of the G5 problem (scalar stress handled through ritual, not chiefs).
sources: Munro & Grosman 2010, PNAS, Early evidence (ca. 12,000 B.P.) for feasting at a burial cave in Israel - https://cris.huji.ac.il/en/publications/early-evidence-ca-12000-bp-for-feasting-at-a-burial-cave-in-israe/

periods_or_stages.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A (PPNA: Khiamian, Sultanian, Mureybetian)
periods_or_stages.dates: ASPRO: 10,200-8,800 cal BC. WF16 (southern Jordan) Bayesian model: about 11,840-10,240 cal BP (about 9,890-8,290 cal BC), most intensive around 11,250 cal BP. Dhra' granaries 11,300-11,175 cal BP.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Round or oval houses in nucleated villages. Wild cereals (barley, wheat) cultivated before they were domesticated: rows of querns at Jerf el Ahmar show large-scale processing of wild cereals. Purpose-built raised-floor granaries at Dhra', placed between houses, about 1,000 years before domestic crops. Communal, partly sunken round buildings at Mureybet and Jerf el Ahmar, used for storage, meetings and ritual. Monumental communal building: Jericho tower, and Göbekli Tepe enclosures (about 9,600/9,500-8,200/8,000 BC) built by hunter-gatherers with feasting. Standardized bead-making in PPNA northeast Jordan (Shubayqa 6), possibly part-time and seasonal, in a non-hierarchical society.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Core G1, plus the start of G2 (wild cereals cultivated, not yet domesticated). Storage is communal or shared, not household-owned, which is the baseline for G4. Large-scale cooperation (monuments, feasts) without visible leaders is relevant to G5. Some craft specialization already exists here (relevant to G3), so it does not depend on surplus.

periods_or_stages.name: Early PPNB (EPPNB)
periods_or_stages.dates: ASPRO: 8,800-7,600 cal BC for PPNB ancien (often narrowed to about 8,700/8,500-8,200 BC; the PPNA/PPNB boundary is disputed and later in the south). Early PPNB at Tell Qarassa North about 8,500-8,300 cal BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Change from round to rectangular houses. First morphologically domestic cereals. Zeder (2011): crop and animal management began together, at least 11,500 cal BP. Pig management in southeast Anatolia by about 10,500-10,000 BP; cattle on the upper Euphrates about 11,000-10,000 BP. Bidirectional naviform blade technology on imported high-quality flint, possibly spread by travelling specialists.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G2 (畑と家畜). In Flannery's model, the change from round huts with shared storage to rectangular nuclear-family houses with their own storerooms happens here. So the start of household property (G4) is already in the PPNB, well before pottery (G3).

periods_or_stages.name: Middle PPNB (MPPNB), including Zagros goat herding (Ganj Dareh)
periods_or_stages.dates: ASPRO: 7,600-6,900 cal BC for PPNB moyen. Other schemes put the MPPNB around 8,300/8,200-7,500 BC. Ganj Dareh goat management about 10,000 cal BP (about 8,000 cal BC).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Goat herding at Ganj Dareh, recognized by the selective culling of young males rather than by smaller bones. Managed goats reached the southern ends of the Fertile Crescent by about 9,500 BP, and sheep 500-1,000 years later. Domestic crops become dominant, but wild resources and hunting continue. Plastered or modelled skulls and the 'Ain Ghazal statues show household and lineage ancestor cults. Rectangular single-family houses with plastered floors. 'Ain Ghazal MPPNB population about 700-900 (Rollefson).
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Mature G2: farming and herding become the core economy. Early G4 signals are household ancestor cults and private storage rooms.
sources: Zeder & Hesse 2000, Science 287:2254-2257, The Initial Domestication of Goats in the Zagros Mountains 10,000 Years Ago - https://doi.org/10.1126/science.287.5461.2254

periods_or_stages.name: Late PPNB mega-sites and the PPNC decline
periods_or_stages.dates: LPPNB about 7,500-7,000/6,700 cal BC. ASPRO groups middle-to-late PPNB plus PPNC as 7,600-6,000 cal BC. PPNC at 'Ain Ghazal 8.9-8.6 cal ka BP (about 6,950-6,650 cal BC). The end of the LPPNB comes 500-800 years before the 8.2 ka event (about 6,200 BC).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Many MPPNB villages abandoned while people gathered into 'mega-sites' of 10-15 ha in the Jordan highlands ('Ain Ghazal, Basta, Wadi Shu'eib, es-Sifiya, 'Ain Jammam). Population estimates of 1,500-4,000 (Rollefson) are disputed: Kuijt argues for hundreds. Single-storey nuclear houses replaced by two-to-three-storey multi-family houses, probably extended families pooling resources, with ground-floor storage. Kadowaki: shared communal labour declined as households grew more independent. Craft specialization: naviform workshops at 'Ain Ghazal, sandstone-ring production at Ba'ja on a household-to-industrial scale, bead and bone workshops at Beidha, mass lime-plaster production. Rollefson describes the pressure of fast population growth as scalar stress. Pigs and cattle added. Pressure on land plus drying led to shrinking or abandonment of the mega-sites in the PPNC. They did not develop into later cities.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: End of G2 into G3 and G4. Craft specialists and extended-family households with their own stores appear. G5 pressure (scalar stress) also appears, and the story is a boom and bust, not steady progress. This is a natural end point for a first 'Neolithic village' block.

periods_or_stages.name: Çatalhöyük East (central Anatolian Late Neolithic), a parallel case
periods_or_stages.dates: Start close to 7,100 cal BC (Bayliss et al. 2015, Journal of World Prehistory). Occupation of the East Mound ended just after 6,000 cal BC (Marciniak et al. 2015, Antiquity).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Dense agglomeration of house-based units, with houses of similar size and similar diets for men and women. Hodder describes it as broadly egalitarian, though some 'history houses' with many burials stand out. Population was revised down to about 600-800 at its peak (Kuijt and Marciniak). Pottery appears within its sequence. The final levels show changes in how houses were built and how burials were made.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: A test case for late G2 into G3 and G4. A large farming settlement without clear wealth inequality or leaders shows that size alone does not produce G4 or G5.

periods_or_stages.name: Early Pottery Neolithic (Upper Mesopotamia pre-Halaf / Proto-Hassuna; southern Levant Yarmukian)
periods_or_stages.dates: Steady pottery production in Upper Mesopotamia began about 7,000-6,700 cal BC (Tell Sabi Abyad about 7,000-6,900 BC). Local plant-tempered coarse ware from about 6,700 BC. Southern Levant (Yarmukian) at least several centuries later. Sha'ar Hagolan is given as 6,500-6,000 BC or 5,500-5,000 BC depending on the source, and the calibration status of both ranges is unclear.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: The first pottery was rare, carefully made, painted mineral-tempered ware, often brought in from elsewhere through exchange networks: a prestige or exchange item, not an everyday tool. Everyday local coarse ware spread only after about 6,700 BC. In the Levant, Yarmukian Sha'ar Hagolan (about 20 ha) has large courtyard houses of 250-700 m² with private silo rooms and silo jars, which points to strong household-level storage.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Start of G3 (pottery begins). The real sequence has two steps: (a) rare, exchanged prestige pots, then (b) ordinary household-made pottery. Full-time potters are not needed at this stage. The courtyard houses with silos fit G4 (household stores).

periods_or_stages.name: Hassuna and Samarra (northern and central Mesopotamia, Late Neolithic)
periods_or_stages.dates: Conventional textbook dates: Hassuna about 6,000/5,500-5,000 BC; Samarra about 5,500-4,800 BC (some sources start at 6,000 BC); Tell es-Sawwan about 5,600-5,000 BC. A calibrated framework for the north Mesopotamian Late Neolithic and Chalcolithic runs about 6,500-4,500 cal BC. Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf partly overlap.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Samarran farmers moved onto the dry edges of the alluvial plain using simple irrigation: small canals at Choga Mami and irrigated flax and six-row barley at Tell es-Sawwan. T-shaped buildings of uniform size at Sawwan were used for grain storage, which implies pooled labour or kin-group-owned stores. Defensive walls or ditches with indirect entrances suggest raiding. Grave wealth varies (many alabaster figurines and vessels at Sawwan), read as rising economic and social differentiation, but villages remain largely egalitarian.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G3 (irrigation-based surplus) into G4 (kin-group stores, uneven grave goods). Early signs of G5 appear (organized irrigation labour, defense). This is the bridge into the Ubaid.

periods_or_stages.name: Sabi Abyad 'Burnt Village' (Pre-Halaf/Transitional) and the Halaf culture
periods_or_stages.dates: Sabi Abyad seals, sealings and storehouses about 6,200-6,000 BC. Halaf about 6,100-5,100 BC (Wikipedia) or 6,500-5,500 BC (Metropolitan Museum). Domuztepe about 6,200-5,450 BC. Several recent calibrated syntheses place Halaf proper around 5,900-5,300 cal BC (from memory, not checked in this search).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Around 6,200 BC at Sabi Abyad: large storehouses, round 'tholoi', hundreds of clay sealings with stamp-seal impressions marking ownership and controlled storage, and clay tokens. Akkermans and Duistermaat read these as communal storage shared with mobile herders. Halaf: very fine painted pottery made at production centres and exchanged widely, possibly as prestige goods between local elites. Domuztepe has about 180 seals and seal-like objects and obsidian traded from up to 800 km away. There is little public architecture and no rigid stratification: 'egalitarian but potentially ranked'.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G3 with skilled production centres for fine ware and exchange, and G4 with seals as marks of ownership and controlled stores. It also gives a first form of G6: exchange between villages and the token and seal tools that later become administration.

periods_or_stages.name: Ubaid period (southern Mesopotamia Ubaid 0-4; Northern Ubaid)
periods_or_stages.dates: Southern Ubaid as a whole: about 6,500-3,800 BC (radiometric summary attributed to Carter & Philip 2010; not checked directly). Ubaid 0 (Tell el-Oueili): 7th millennium BC (CNRS), elsewhere 5,500-5,400 BC. Ubaid 1 (Eridu): 5,400-4,700 BC or 5,200-4,800 BC. Ubaid 2 (Hajji Muhammad): about 4,800-4,500 BC. Ubaid 3-4: about 4,500-3,800 BC (sources disagree by several centuries). Northern Ubaid: about 5,300-4,300 BC. Eridu temple level XVII: about 5,300-5,000 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Irrigation farming spreads across the southern alluvium. Standard tripartite houses with a long central hall. A long sequence of temples rebuilt in the same place at Eridu (small shrine, then a platform at level XI, then a tripartite plan from level VIII, then a large complex at level VII about 4,000-3,500 BC). 'Chieftain's houses': Tell Abada Building A, larger and central, held stored pottery, clay tokens kept in vessels, and 57 infant burials. Similar buildings at Tepe Gawra XII and Değirmentepe, with stamp-seal sealings near administrative and cultic buildings. Very uniform pottery across a wide 'interaction sphere' (Carter & Philip; Stein). Graves show little difference in wealth. Stein (1994): chiefly elites in small irrigation polities used inclusive, group-centred ideology and ritually mobilized staple finance. Overt ranking, warfare and exotic prestige goods appear only at the very end. A minority (Akkermans, Forest, Hole) sees the Ubaid as egalitarian.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: The central case for G5 (リーダーと決まり): temple and chief-house leaders, sealing-based control of stores, and dispute settlement inferred. G4 continues (household tripartite storage), but inequality stays deliberately muted. G3 is well developed (standardized pottery). This fits the user's 'Ubaid chiefdoms' anchor.

periods_or_stages.name: Terminal Ubaid / LC1-LC2 and Early Uruk: first towns, northern urbanism
periods_or_stages.dates: Late Chalcolithic overall about 4,600-3,100 BCE (Renette et al. 2022). LC2 at Tell Brak about 4,200-3,800 BC (urban growth possibly from about 4,300 BC). Early Uruk about 4,000-3,800 BC (other schemes 3,900-3,600 or 4,000-3,500 BC).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Tell Brak grows to about 55 ha with a ring of satellite settlements. It already has monumental buildings, industrial-scale production and prestige goods in the late 5th millennium, so urbanism did not start only in the south (Oates et al. 2007). Bevel-rim bowls, made in moulds and widely read as ration measures, appear in Early Uruk in the south.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Start of G6 (a town) on top of a mature G5. This is the start of a 'state and town' block.

periods_or_stages.name: Middle Uruk / LC3-LC4: regional hierarchy and expansion
periods_or_stages.dates: About 3,800-3,400 BC (one older scheme instead runs Early Uruk to 3,500 BC). Tell Brak LC3 about 3,800-3,400 BC. Purely numerical tablets about 3,500-3,350 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Tell Brak reaches about 130 ha. Mass graves at Brak (about 3,800-3,600 BC) suggest violence during urban growth. In the Susiana plain, settlement-size hierarchies and administrative tiers appear: Johnson and Wright explain state formation as driven by rising information-processing and administrative needs, after testing and rejecting simple population-pressure models. Accounting tools spread: tokens, hollow clay balls holding tokens, and bullae sealed with cylinder seals, then numerical tablets. The Uruk expansion begins.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G6 (trade, town, records) building on G5. Corresponds to the 'tokens' step of G6, before true writing.

periods_or_stages.name: Late Uruk (Uruk V-IVa) / LC5, then Jemdet Nasr (Uruk III)
periods_or_stages.dates: Late Uruk about 3,400-3,100 BC; recent radiocarbon work suggests it ended closer to about 3,300 BC. Uruk IV proto-cuneiform tablets about 3,350-3,200 BC. Uruk III / Jemdet Nasr about 3,200-3,000 BC. The full proto-cuneiform corpus (about 5,000 tablets) dates about 3,350-3,000 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Uruk is the first real city: about 250 ha by about 3,200 BC (some sources say 300 ha), with tens of thousands of people (40,000-80,000 in popular sources; uncertain). Two monumental temple districts (Eanna and Anu). Mass-produced bevel-rim bowls make up about 75% of pottery and are read as ration bowls. Cylinder seals. Uruk 'colonies' and outposts on the Euphrates (Habuba Kabira, Jebel Aruda), 20-40 ha, inside a core-periphery exchange network (Algaze). Proto-cuneiform administrative tablets, including the Standard Professions List (Lu2 A), already show ranked occupations and titles.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: End of G6 (交易・町・記録): writing, a city, long-distance trade, and a specialized, ranked workforce. The natural end point of 'Society 2.0'.

periods_or_stages.name: Model stages (not a chronological period): Flannery's household sequence
periods_or_stages.dates: n/a. Approximate archaeological fit: stage 1 in the Natufian and PPNA; stage 2 in the EPPNB and MPPNB; stage 3 in the LPPNB, and later in Ubaid-style tripartite houses.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Stage 1: small round huts with shared or communal storage. Stage 2: nuclear families in larger rectangular houses with private storerooms. Stage 3: extended-family households with larger workforces and more varied economies.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: A ready-made way to split G4 into steps: shared stores, then household stores, then extended-household estates with inheritance. In the Near East this starts much earlier than G3 pottery, so the simulation could seed G4 behaviour from G2 onward.

periods_or_stages.name: Model stages (not a chronological period): labour-limited to land-limited farming and inequality (Bogaard, Fochesato & Bowles; Kohler et al.)
periods_or_stages.dates: n/a. Wealth inequality stayed modest for at least four millennia after the start of farming, then rose with plough and animal traction ('secondary products', mainly 4th millennium BC in the Near East).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Gini coefficients from house size, storage size and grave goods across 90 site-phases in western Eurasia: land-limited (plough, traction) systems are much more unequal than labour-limited (hoe) ones. Kohler et al. 2017 (63 sites, house-size Gini): inequality generally rises with domestication and political scale, and keeps rising in Eurasia because of large domesticable animals. A 2025 PNAS special feature found only a slight rise with the start of farming.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Suggests splitting G4 into G4a 'property exists' (PPNB to Halaf, low Gini) and G4b 'property becomes unequal' (late Ubaid to Uruk, plough, herds, land scarcity). Large Gini values should not appear right after G2.

major_breakpoints: 1. Sedentism before farming, about 15,000-14,500 cal BP (Early Natufian). Villages and population growth start while people still forage, so G1 really does come first. Sources: Bar-Yosef 1998, Evolutionary Anthropology; Richter et al. 2017, Scientific Reports.

2. The 'Neolithic Revolution' (Childe), PPNA to EPPNB, about 11,700-10,200 cal BP: wild cereals cultivated (Dhra' granaries 11,300 cal BP; Jerf el Ahmar), then domestication. Plant domestication was slow: non-shattering wheat appears about 9,500 BP but wild types still dominate fields at 7,500 BP (Tanno & Willcox 2006, Science, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16574859/). Fuller et al. (2012) estimate about 4,000 years, which is disputed. Zeder 2011 places crop and animal management together at least 11,500 cal BP. Bocquet-Appel 2011 (Science 333:560) adds a Neolithic Demographic Transition of about +2 births per woman, a direct driver of G1-G2 population growth.

3. Household privatization, PPNA to PPNB (about 8,800-7,500 BC): round huts with shared storage give way to rectangular houses with private storerooms, and later to extended-family houses (Flannery 1972/2002; Byrd 1994, American Antiquity 59:639-666). This is when G4 property begins, before pottery.

4. LPPNB mega-sites and their breakdown, about 7,500-6,500 BC: aggregation, scalar stress, extended households and craft specialists, then shrinking or abandonment in the PPNC (8.9-8.6 cal ka BP). The breakdown comes before the 8.2 ka climate event. Many scholars treat it as a reset, not a step toward cities (Kuijt 2000; Kadowaki 2012; Zielhofer et al. 2012). Natural end of a first sub-era.

5. Pottery and the Late Neolithic, about 7,000-6,700 cal BC in Upper Mesopotamia: first prestige or exchanged pots, then household coarse ware after 6,700 BC (Leiden Sabi Abyad project). This is a technology change more than a social one.

6. Seals, sealings and controlled storage, about 6,200-6,000 BC (Sabi Abyad), then Halaf stamp seals and long-distance exchange. These are the first administrative marks of ownership, and the origin of the G6 accounting tools.

7. Irrigation colonization of the alluvium, Samarra and Ubaid 0 (7th to early 6th millennium BC), then Ubaid temples and chief houses (about 5,300-4,000 BC; Stein 1994; Carter & Philip 2010). This is the main point where formal leadership (G5) appears.

8. The 'Urban Revolution' (Childe 1950), about 4,200-3,100 BC: northern towns first (Tell Brak LC2, 55 ha, about 4,200 BC; Oates et al. 2007), then southern Uruk (about 250 ha) with state-level administrative hierarchy (Wright & Johnson 1975; Johnson 1973). Writing appears about 3,350-3,200 BC (Uruk IV). Childe's two 'revolutions' (Neolithic and Urban) are the two biggest consensus breaks. Breakpoints 4 and 7 are the most defensible intermediate breaks.
critiques_or_caveats: The G1-G6 order does not match the Near Eastern record in places. Household storage and property (G4) start in the PPNB, about 1,500-2,000 years before pottery (G3). Craft specialization (beads, naviform blades, lime plaster, sandstone rings) is already present in the PPNA and PPNB, sometimes in non-hierarchical societies with no clear surplus link (Shubayqa 6 bead study; Barzilai). A strict order of 'surplus, then craft, then property' is a simplification.

Large-scale cooperation came before leaders. Göbekli Tepe (about 9,600-8,200 BC), the Jericho tower and the PPNA communal buildings were built by communities with no visible elites, coordinated through feasting and ritual. A G5 model where coordination needs a leader is not supported for early periods.

Inequality was slow and non-linear. Bogaard et al. 2019 find wealth inequality modest for at least four millennia after farming began. The 2025 PNAS GINI feature finds only a slight rise with farming. Çatalhöyük (about 7,100-6,000 cal BC) had similar house sizes. Ubaid elites may have deliberately hidden their status, so graves show little difference (Stein 1994; Kopanias & Barlagianni). Varna (AMS about 4,560-4,450 cal BC; Higham et al. 2007, Antiquity) is in the Balkans, not the Near East, and should only be a comparison.

The sequence was not steady progress. The LPPNB mega-sites shrank or were abandoned, and Neolithic mega-sites did not lead to Bronze Age cities (Kadowaki 2012; Düring; Gebel). Late Natufian groups may have become more mobile again. Uruk outposts collapsed at the end of the expansion. A simulation could allow setbacks.

Dating problems. Many ranges (Hassuna, Samarra, Halaf, Ubaid 0-5, Early/Middle/Late Uruk) are ceramic-phase dates, and sources disagree by 300-1,000 years. Example: Ubaid 0 is placed in the 7th millennium BC by CNRS but at 5,500-5,400 BC elsewhere, and the Ubaid 4 dates conflict. The PPNA/PPNB boundary is later in the south than in the north. Göbekli Tepe dates were revised because of old-wood effects. LC1 and the LC5-to-Early Bronze boundary have few radiocarbon dates.

Disputed population sizes. LPPNB mega-site estimates of 1,500-4,000 (Rollefson) against 'hundreds' (Kuijt). Çatalhöyük revised to about 600-800. Uruk at 40,000-80,000 comes mostly from popular sources.

The tokens-to-writing theory (Schmandt-Besserat 1992) is influential but contested. Tokens continued alongside writing, and the token evidence at Sabi Abyad does not show one universal accounting role. Bevel-rim bowls as ration bowls is also disputed: residue work at Shakhi Kora found meat stews.

The 'colonies' and 'world system' labels for the Uruk expansion (Algaze) are contested in favour of more local agency. Stein and others argue the Ubaid spread by copying, not colonization. Ubaid as chiefdom versus egalitarian is unresolved; the chiefdom view is the mainstream one.

Ganj Dareh (Zagros, about 10,000 cal BP, about 8,000 BC) is not the earliest animal management: Zeder 2011 places management at least 11,500 cal BP, and cattle and pigs in Anatolia and Syria around 11,000-10,000 BP. Ganj Dareh is the clearest demographic-culling evidence, not the start date.
research.notes:
How to split 'Society 2.0', based on the breaks above.

Option A, three blocks following Childe's two revolutions plus the PPNB reset:
- 2.0a 'Neolithic village': Natufian to LPPNB, about 12,700-6,500 BC. Covers G1, G2, plus early household storage and part-time crafts.
- 2.0b 'Late Neolithic and Chalcolithic village and chiefdom': Pottery Neolithic, Hassuna/Samarra, Halaf, Ubaid, about 7,000-4,200 BC. Covers G3, G4, G5.
- 2.0c 'Urban revolution': LC2 to Late Uruk, about 4,200-3,100 BC. Covers G6.

Option B, four blocks (more balanced): split 2.0b at about 6,200-5,500 BC into:
- 'Pottery, seals and exchange villages' (Pottery Neolithic to Halaf; G3 and G4a)
- 'Irrigation, temples and chiefs' (Samarra to Ubaid; G4b and G5)

Suggested sub-steps for the running G3, each with an archaeological anchor:
- G3-1: rare, exchanged prestige pots (Sabi Abyad, about 7,000-6,700 cal BC).
- G3-2: household-made coarse ware for storage and cooking (from about 6,700 BC).
- G3-3: skilled production centres for fine ware traded between villages (Halaf, about 6,000-5,300 BC).
- G3-4: standardized or mass-produced ware (Ubaid uniformity, then Uruk bevel-rim bowls about 3,900-3,100 BC).

Possible splits of G4:
- G4a: shared stores, then household stores (PPNB, Flannery stage 2).
- G4b: extended-household and kin-group estates, seals as ownership marks (LPPNB, Sabi Abyad, Halaf).
- G4c: land-limited, plough-based inequality with high Gini (late Ubaid to Uruk, Bogaard et al. 2019).

Johnson 1982 ('Organizational structure and scalar stress', in Renfrew, Rowlands & Segraves eds., Theory and Explanation in Archaeology, pp. 389-421; https://mapaspects.org/biblio/ref_4260/index.html) proposes a threshold of about 6 basal units before a group splits or builds a hierarchy. This was confirmed only at abstract level, and it could be used directly as a G5 trigger.

Limits of this research:
- WebFetch was blocked for Wikipedia, PMC and isac.uchicago.edu, so several claims rest on search-result abstracts and summaries, not full texts.
- The calibrated Halaf range of about 5,900-5,300 cal BC is from memory and was not checked.
- The Yarmukian calibrated range was not established: the sources conflict and do not say whether their dates are calibrated.
- The Younger Dryas dates (about 12,900-11,700 BP) were not checked.
- The exact year of the Willcox & Stordeur Antiquity article (2012 vs 2014) was not confirmed.
- The Shubayqa 6 part-time bead-craft study is real per the search results, but its author and year were not captured.
- Some feature details come from popular or secondary pages; those sources are labelled as such: Jewish Virtual Library for Sha'ar Hagolan, World History Encyclopedia for Çatalhöyük, popular pages for Uruk population, TOEFL-type passages for bevel-rim bowl production (the last are not cited above).

research.lens: Theories of social evolution and political organization: Service (band, tribe, chiefdom, state), Fried (egalitarian, rank, stratified, state), Johnson & Earle (family-level group, local group, regional polity), Flannery (1972 processes; 2002 village stages) and Flannery & Marcus (2012), Johnson 1982 scalar stress, Wright & Johnson on state formation, Earle and Carneiro on chiefdoms, and critiques (Feinman & Neitzel, Yoffee, Graeber & Wengrow, Hodder, M. L. Smith). Each stage is matched to its Near Eastern archaeological correlate and to the simulation phases G1-G6.

periods_or_stages.name: Service 'band' = Fried 'egalitarian (mobile)' = Johnson & Earle 'family-level group'. Near East correlate: Epipaleolithic (Kebaran/Geometric Kebaran) foragers
periods_or_stages.dates: before c. 15,000 cal BP (the Early Natufian is dated c. 13,400-11,800 BC by PPND)
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Small, kin-based, mobile foraging units with no formal government. Under Fried, prestige rests on age, sex and ability and is open to everyone. Johnson & Earle make the family the main economic unit. Archaeological correlates: small seasonal camps, flimsy huts, little or no storage, no differences between dwellings.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Before G1. This is the simulation's starting condition, and G1 begins when people leave this stage by settling down.

periods_or_stages.name: Natufian hamlets: the start of the Johnson & Earle 'local group' (sedentary egalitarian) and the first scalar stress
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 15,000-11,700 cal BP (c. 13,000-9,750 BCE). The start and end dates are disputed by about 200-500 years.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Semi-sedentary or sedentary hamlets with round, semi-subterranean houses and burials inside the settlement. Communities were small: Kuijt (2000), as cited in a later paper, estimates about 60 people per site. A Current Anthropology article on the Natufian (Univ. of Chicago Press) says scalar stress in Johnson's 1982 sense appears from the start of the Early Natufian. There are no formal leaders, and the society is egalitarian in Fried's sense.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G1 (村ができる). Sedentism plus births and immigrants push the community toward the first scalar-stress thresholds.
sources: Kuijt 2000, J. Anthropological Archaeology 19:75-102, 'People and Space in Early Agricultural Villages', https://arheo.ffzg.unizg.hr/ska/tekstovi/people_space.pdf

periods_or_stages.name: PPNA villages: local group with communal storage and a 'sequential' (consensual) hierarchy (Flannery 2002 village stage 1)
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 11,700-10,700 cal BP (c. 9,750-8,750 BCE). The PPNA/PPNB boundary varies by region from about 8,800 to 8,250 BCE.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Small round-to-oval buildings with shared or communal storage (Flannery 2002, stage 1). Communal and ritual buildings and monumental enclosures. Communities of about 330 people (Kuijt 2000, as reported by others). Wild cereals were cultivated before morphological domestication. Watkins (2023) argues that the scalar stress of permanent aggregation was spread out through communal construction of monumental buildings, shared symbolism and more intense communal ritual. In Johnson's terms this is integration by consensus, not by permanent chiefs. Johnson & Earle's 'family and village' and 'village and clan'. Service's 'tribe' (segmentary, no permanent offices).
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Late G1 into early G2. The village grows past 'face-to-face' size, and cultivation becomes important.
sources: Flannery 2002, 'The Origins of the Village Revisited: From Nuclear to Extended Households', American Antiquity, https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/98E6C778190FEE73A0EC2EF55635659F
Watkins 2023, Frontiers in Human Dynamics (author attribution taken from a search summary), https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/human-dynamics/articles/10.3389/fhumd.2023.1250167/full
Pre-Pottery Neolithic A overview, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Pottery_Neolithic_A

periods_or_stages.name: PPNB villages: household-based 'local group' with achievement-based prestige (Flannery 2002 stage 2; Flannery & Marcus 'achievement-based society'; Johnson & Earle 'corporate group and big-man collectivity')
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 10,700-8,250 cal BP (c. 8,750-6,300 BCE). Çatalhöyük in Anatolia is later, c. 7100-6000 BCE.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Rectangular multi-room houses, each holding a nuclear family with its own storage (Flannery 2002, stage 2). Byrd (1994) frames this as a shift between public and private, and between domestic and corporate space. The household becomes the unit of production and storage. Cereals and caprines were domesticated (e.g. goats at Ganj Dareh), and the earliest simple clay tokens come from Ganj Dareh and Tepe Asiab (Schmandt-Besserat). Late PPNB villages grew large: Kuijt 2000, as reported by others, gives about 765 people in the early PPNB and 3,000-4,000 later, though Kuijt has since argued for hundreds rather than thousands. Many large villages broke up around 8,500-8,000 BP, which Kuijt links to 'social crowding'. At Çatalhöyük, households hold similar wealth in most levels, and inequality appears only after about 6500 BC. Hodder (2022) treats 'staying egalitarian' as an active process: a tension between communal ('molar') and household-autonomous ('molecular') tendencies, with the latter growing alongside agricultural intensification. Under Fried the society is still egalitarian. Under Flannery & Marcus, prestige can be achieved but not inherited.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G2 (畑と家畜) at its core. It also lays the base for G4: private household storage is the material precondition for household property.

periods_or_stages.name: Pottery Neolithic: Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf. Fried's transition from egalitarian to rank; Frangipane's 'horizontal' vs 'vertical' egalitarian societies
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 6,300-5,000 BCE (≈ 8,250-7,000 cal BP). An Oxford chronology gives the Pottery Neolithic as c. 6300-5200 BC. Sabi Abyad levels date to c. 5700-5000 BC. Samarra is c. 5500-4800 BCE according to an encyclopedia entry.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Pottery, then fine painted wares (Halaf) that imply specialist production. Stamp seals and clay sealings on baskets and jars at Tell Sabi Abyad: 27 design types, and sealings kept as records of stored goods. Akkermans & Duistermaat read this as communal storage shared with mobile groups, which means administration of stores existed before formal leaders. Samarra-culture irrigation at Tell es-Sawwan and rich alabaster grave goods. Frangipane (2007) contrasts Halaf 'horizontal egalitarian' systems (no hierarchy) with Samarra and Ubaid 'vertical egalitarian' systems, where privileged status coexists with substantial equality. In Fried's terms, the first permanent positions of prestige appear without economic power.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G3 (余りと分業): pottery and part-time crafts. It also covers the first half of G4 (持ち物と差): seals mark ownership and control of stored goods, while wealth differences stay small.

periods_or_stages.name: Ubaid: Fried's 'rank society', Service's 'chiefdom', Johnson & Earle's 'simple chiefdom / regional polity'. The interpretation is disputed.
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 5500-4000 BCE across Mesopotamia, beginning in the southern alluvium c. 6200 BCE (Met Museum). This is ≈ 8,150-5,950 cal BP.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: The Met notes that some villages grew into towns centered on monumental buildings (e.g. Eridu and Uruk); the repeatedly rebuilt temples at Eridu are standard textbook knowledge but were not verified in the sources I reached. Irrigation farming. A two-tier settlement pattern, with relatively large settlements serving as centers for groups of smaller ones. Stein (1994) treats the chiefdom as a useful model. He describes small irrigation-based polities whose elites used an inclusive ideology and ritually organized staple finance. Warfare and exotic long-distance trade appear only at the very end of the roughly 1,500-year Ubaid. Flannery & Marcus date hereditary aristocracies in the Near East to about 7,500 years ago. Definitions in use: Carneiro (1981) defines a chiefdom as an autonomous multi-village unit under a permanent paramount chief. Wright (1977, as cited) gives it one or two control levels above the local community. Earle (1997) describes kin-based rank with staple or wealth finance and a few thousand to tens of thousands of people. Counter-evidence: Kopanias & Barlagianni find little variation in Ubaid grave goods and few prestige goods. Graeber & Wengrow suggest an 'overt ideology of equality'.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G5 (リーダーと決まり). The leaders here are ritual and managerial, not wealthy, and they integrate several villages. This fits Blanton et al.'s 'corporate' strategy better than an exclusionary one.

periods_or_stages.name: Fried's 'stratified society': unequal access to strategic resources (economic stratification)
periods_or_stages.dates: n/a as a type. Near-East and Western Eurasian correlates mostly date from the late 5th to the 4th millennium BCE. Varna (Balkans) dates to the mid-5th millennium BC, and the steep rise in Eurasian inequality comes from about 4000 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Fried's type: some people have unrestricted access to land, water and herds while others face restrictions, so economic differences appear even among people of similar rank. Fried holds that ranking usually comes before stratification. Correlates: house-size Gini coefficients (Kohler et al. 2017 find inequality rising with domestication and with political scale). The GINI project (PNAS special feature, 2025) finds that inequality often rose significantly only millennia after farming began, and only in some places. Bogaard, Fochesato & Bowles (2019) find land-limited farming systems far more unequal than labour-limited ones, and press coverage links the rise from about 4000 BC to ox-drawn ploughs. Price & Bar-Yosef (2010) argue that traces of inequality appear at the origins of agriculture.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: The 'difference' half of G4 (持ち物と差). In Fried's order and in the Near Eastern evidence, strong wealth stratification comes after institutional rank and leadership (Ubaid temples) and grows in the Late Ubaid and Uruk periods. G4 might therefore be split, with the wealth-inequality part placed after or alongside G5.

periods_or_stages.name: Uruk: 'archaic state' (Service, Fried, Johnson & Earle), with Wright & Johnson's administrative-hierarchy criterion
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 4000-3100 BCE (≈ 5,950-5,050 cal BP). Early Uruk is c. 4000-3500 and Late Uruk c. 3500-3100. CDLI gives 4000-3000, and Algaze uses 3800-3100. Proto-cuneiform accounting texts date to the late 4th millennium BCE (c. 3300-3100).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Wright & Johnson (1975): a specialized local administrative system and a local exchange network appear at the start of Early Uruk on the Susiana plain. Johnson (1973) treats rising information-processing needs as a major cause. State criterion as usually cited: three or more administrative levels above the community, or a four-tier settlement hierarchy (Wright 1977; Johnson 1982 and 1987). Susiana had a four-tier settlement-size hierarchy. Uruk-Warka reached about 100 ha in the Uruk period (CDLI). Larger figures such as 250 ha were not verified. The recording sequence runs from complex tokens to sealed clay envelopes (bullae) to numerical tablets to proto-cuneiform. In Algaze's 'Uruk expansion', colonies and outposts secured trade. Graeber & Wengrow stress temple bureaucracy and assemblies, with no clear evidence of an autocratic king early on.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G6 (交易・町・記録). The context's 'Uruk ~5300 BP' corresponds to Late Uruk.
sources: Wright & Johnson 1975, American Anthropologist 77(2):267-289 (summary), https://acawiki.org/Population,_Exchange,_and_Early_State_Formation_in_Southwestern_Iran
Johnson 1973, Local Exchange and Early State Development in Southwestern Iran, https://press.umich.edu/Books/L/Local-Exchange-and-Early-State-Development-in-Southwestern-Iran
CDLI, Uruk (mod. Warka), https://cdli.ox.ac.uk/wiki/uruk_mod._warka
Algaze 2001 essay summary (eHRAF), https://ehrafarchaeology.yale.edu/traditions/mh60/documents/019
Schmandt-Besserat 1977, https://undena.com/EL-UP/Schmandt_Besserat_1977_Archaic_Recording_System_-_SMS_1.2.pdf
Yale SOM on proto-cuneiform accounting, https://som.yale.edu/story/2023/prof-goetzmann-discusses-finance-practices-mesopotamia
Paper on Zapotec state formation citing Wright's four-tier criterion (PNAS; PMC2867764)

periods_or_stages.name: Johnson 1982 scalar stress: sequential (consensual) vs simultaneous (permanent) hierarchy
periods_or_stages.dates: n/a (a mechanism). Near-East applications run from the Early Natufian to the PPNB, and the state criterion applies in the Uruk period.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Communication and decision stress grows exponentially with the number of basal units. At about six units, groups tend to subdivide or add a hierarchical level. Dispute frequency rises with scalar-communications stress. There are two responses. (1) Sequential hierarchy: egalitarian consensus, with larger basal units (e.g. households grouped into extended families or lineages) and ritual or feasting integration. (2) Simultaneous hierarchy: institutionalized permanent decision-makers, with control and status differences growing with the number of levels. Village fission is the third option. Archaeological correlates include communal buildings and feasting, standardized ritual, house-cluster size, fission or abandonment of large villages, and the number of settlement tiers.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: The driver from G1 to G5. It implies that G5 has two sub-steps: consensus councils and ritual integration first, then permanent leaders and punishments. The '6 basal units' threshold is directly simulatable.
sources: Johnson 1982, 'Organizational structure and scalar stress', in Renfrew, Rowlands & Segraves (eds), Theory and Explanation in Archaeology, pp. 389-421 (abstract), https://mapaspects.org/biblio/ref_4260/index.html
Alberti 2014, PLoS ONE, modelling group size and scalar stress, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3953443/
Kuijt 2000, https://arheo.ffzg.unizg.hr/ska/tekstovi/people_space.pdf

periods_or_stages.name: Flannery 1972 processes (segregation and centralization) and Blanton et al. 1996 'corporate' vs 'network' strategies
periods_or_stages.dates: n/a (processes and strategies, not stages)
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Flannery 1972 treats state formation as two processes rather than fixed stages. Segregation is the growing differentiation of subsystems, and centralization is the concentration of control; both act through mechanisms such as promotion and linearization. Blanton, Feinman, Kowalewski & Peregrine (1996) describe two ends of a continuum of leadership strategy. Network (exclusionary) leaders rely on outside ties, esoteric knowledge and prestige goods. Corporate leaders build on kin and group membership and act as 'first among equals'. Ubaid, with its inclusive ideology and staple finance (Stein), looks corporate.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G5 and G6. These are parameters for how leaders arise and finance themselves (staple vs wealth finance, corporate vs network), not extra phases.
sources: Flannery 1972, 'The Cultural Evolution of Civilizations', Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics 3:399-426, https://www.mapaspects.org/biblio/ref_1711/index.html
Blanton et al. 1996, Current Anthropology 37(1):1-14, https://www2.lawrence.edu/fast/PEREGRIP/Publications/dual_processual.pdf

major_breakpoints: Sedentism and village formation, c. 15,000-11,700 cal BP (Natufian into PPNA). Scalar stress appears as soon as people aggregate permanently. Sources: Johnson 1982; Natufian article in Current Anthropology (Univ. Chicago Press) https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/reader/10.1086/658861; Kuijt 2000 https://arheo.ffzg.unizg.hr/ska/tekstovi/people_space.pdf

Communal storage gives way to household storage, c. 10,700 cal BP (PPNA to PPNB). Round huts with shared storage are replaced by rectangular nuclear-family houses with private stores, and the household becomes the economic and property unit. Sources: Flannery 2002 https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/98E6C778190FEE73A0EC2EF55635659F; Byrd 1994 American Antiquity 59(4)
Aggregation crisis, c. 8,500-8,000 cal BP (Late PPNB). Large villages break up under 'social crowding', which shows that growth can reverse instead of leading to hierarchy. Source: Kuijt 2000

Administration before chiefs, c. 6,300-5,000 BCE (Pottery Neolithic, Halaf, Samarra). Pottery and craft specialists appear, stamp seals and sealings control stored goods (Sabi Abyad, c. 5700-5000 BC), and Frangipane identifies 'horizontal' vs 'vertical' egalitarian paths. Sources: Frangipane 2007 https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/93529; Akkermans & Duistermaat 1996

Hereditary rank and chiefdom-like polities, about 7,500 years ago (c. 5500 BCE, Samarra and Ubaid). Temples at Eridu, a two-tier settlement pattern and ritual staple finance appear. Sources: Flannery & Marcus 2012 https://themontrealreview.com/2009/The-Creation-of-Inequality.php; Stein 1994 https://ehrafarchaeology.yale.edu/traditions/mh55/documents/004; Met Ubaid essay https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/the-ubaid-period-5500-4000-b-c

Wealth stratification takes off from about 4000 BC in Western Eurasia, linked to land-limited farming and ox ploughs. Inequality often rises only millennia after farming begins. Sources: Bogaard et al. 2019 https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antiquity/article/abs/farminginequality-nexus-new-insights-from-ancient-western-eurasia/8EFE3B8F5AFA07450F87E4E9B553A43E; Kohler et al. 2017 doi:10.1038/nature24646; GINI/PNAS 2025

State formation at the start of Early Uruk, c. 4000-3500 BCE: specialized administration, three or more administrative levels and a four-tier settlement hierarchy. Writing follows c. 3300-3100 BCE (proto-cuneiform, Late Uruk). Sources: Wright & Johnson 1975 https://acawiki.org/Population,_Exchange,_and_Early_State_Formation_in_Southwestern_Iran; Wright 1977; Johnson 1973; CDLI https://cdli.ox.ac.uk/wiki/uruk_mod._warka
critiques_or_caveats: Typological critique: Feinman & Neitzel (1984), 'Too many types', found that traits used to diagnose chiefdoms vary independently and continuously. Many archaeologists now group tribes and chiefdoms together as 'middle-range societies' and analyze variables (scale, hierarchy, inequality, integration) rather than boxes. Sources: https://pennds.org/archaeobib/items/show/25815; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociopolitical_typology

Yoffee (2005), Myths of the Archaic State: neo-evolutionary ladders 'stifled rather than stimulated' research on early states. Early Mesopotamian cities combined heterarchy with hierarchy, and the state is not the end point of a fixed sequence. https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9780511489662/type/book

Graeber & Wengrow (2021), The Dawn of Everything: societies switched seasonally between hierarchical and egalitarian arrangements, and they chose their political forms; farming does not dictate politics. On Mesopotamia they suggest an Ubaid 'ideology of equality' and assemblies in Uruk. Critics (e.g. Publishers Weekly, New Politics, the Cliodynamics special issue) say the book generalizes from thin evidence. https://www.historynewsnetwork.org/article/review-digging-for-utopia; https://journalpub.escholarship.org/cliodynamics/article/38332/galley/28827/download

Calling the Ubaid a chiefdom is contested. Stein (1994) keeps the chiefdom model with ritual staple finance, but Kopanias & Barlagianni find almost no mortuary or prestige-good evidence for stratification. Any 'leader' phase in the simulation should not require visible wealth differences. https://www.archaeopresspublishing.com/ojs/index.php/ash-sharq/article/view/711

Hodder (2022): equality in the Neolithic was actively maintained. Communal and household-autonomy tendencies were in tension, so inequality does not follow automatically from surplus. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0959774322000063

Inequality is not a simple function of farming, population or aggregation. Gini values rose only after millennia, and only in some places (GINI project, PNAS 2025). This argues against tying G4 directly to G2 or G3.

Settlement-size hierarchies, the main archaeological test for chiefdom vs state, are criticized as unreliable. Surface-survey data are problematic, and smaller sites acted autonomously (Monica L. Smith 2021, World Archaeology). https://anthro.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/2021-Smith-Site-Size-Hierarchies.pdf

A linear path from 'small-scale egalitarian' to 'large-scale stratified' may not exist even in Mesopotamia (Başur Höyük study, Cambridge Archaeological Journal 2025). https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/cambridge-archaeological-journal/article/inequality-at-the-dawn-of-the-bronze-age-the-case-of-basur-hoyuk-a-royal-cemetery-at-the-margins-of-the-mesopotamian-world/19A5E0FB47541DB5B43BF8C5E93B7533

Counterpoint, and the current mainstream position: stages are kept as heuristic shorthand, not as laws. Turchin et al. (2018, Seshat) found that one principal component explains about three-quarters of the variance across 51 complexity variables in 414 societies, so traits co-vary strongly even though societies form a continuum rather than discrete types. A 2026 article in Historická sociologie judges Johnson & Earle's scale-based scheme the most useful because it avoids contested terms like 'tribe'. https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10041342/; https://karolinum.cz/data/clanek/17473/HS_18_1_0089.pdf

The ordering problem for this simulation: Fried's scheme and the Near Eastern evidence put rank and leadership (Ubaid temples, c. 5500 BCE) before strong economic stratification (late 5th to 4th millennium BCE). The current G4 (property and inequality) then G5 (leaders) order reverses the 'inequality' half of that sequence.
research.notes:
PROPOSAL FOR SPLITTING 'Society 2.0' (to discuss with the user):
Option A, three acts following Johnson & Earle's scale levels (my recommendation):
(2-1) 村の社会 / Local village, Natufian to PPNB, c. 15,000-8,250 cal BP. Covers G1 and G2. The society is egalitarian, the household replaces communal storage, and scalar stress is handled by ritual or by village fission.
(2-2) 家と余りの社会 / Households and surplus, Pottery Neolithic to Halaf/Samarra, c. 6300-5000 BCE. Covers G3 and G4a. Pottery and craft specialists appear, seals control stores, and household property and inheritance develop, while wealth differences stay small. Frangipane's horizontal vs vertical egalitarian paths could be a branch point here.
(2-3) 首長と町の社会 / Regional polity, Ubaid to Uruk, c. 5500-3100 BCE. Covers G5, G4b and G6: ritual or consensual leaders, then permanent chiefs, then wealth stratification, then the state with three or more administrative levels, and finally writing.
Option B, Fried's four checkpoints: egalitarian (G1-G3) / rank (G5a) / stratified (G4b) / state (G6).

Measurable milestones the simulation could use as sub-steps: village size of about 60, then about 300, then about 700 or more (Kuijt's figures, secondhand); more than about 6 basal units triggering a new decision level (Johnson 1982); share of private vs communal storage (Flannery 2002); seal or token use; number of settlement tiers going from 1 to 2 to 3 to 4; house-size Gini (Kohler 2017).

Suggested internal splits:
- G4 into G4a 'household property and inheritance' (PPNB to Halaf) and G4b 'wealth stratification' (Late Ubaid to Uruk, c. 4000 BC, ox-plough and land-limited farming).
- G5 into G5a 'sequential/consensual hierarchy' (councils, ritual, dispute settlement by elders) and G5b 'simultaneous hierarchy' (permanent chiefs, punishment, staple finance).

SOURCE CAVEATS:
- WebFetch was blocked for Wikipedia, the Met, MIT OCW and PMC. Most claims therefore come from search-result abstracts, catalogue records and secondary summaries, not full texts.
- Kuijt's population figures (60, 330, 765, 3,000-4,000) are as reported by a later paper, and Kuijt has since revised the large-village estimates downward.
- Attributing the Frontiers 2023 paper to Watkins comes from a search summary.
- The PNAS paper citing Wright's four-tier criterion (PMC2867764) is probably Spencer 2010 on Zapotec state formation; not verified.
- Whether Wright 1977 or Johnson 1982/1987 is the origin of the 'three or more administrative levels' criterion is reported inconsistently in secondary sources.
- The Uruk size of 250 ha is unverified (CDLI says about 100 ha).
- The Met essay is from 2003. The Eridu temple sequence is standard knowledge but was not verified in the retrieved text.
- Flannery & Marcus's detailed Near Eastern case studies, such as PPN 'men's houses', were not verified. Only the quoted 7,500-year date for hereditary aristocracy was seen.
- Price & Bar-Yosef's 2010 date was not confirmed from the catalogue record.
- Halaf dates vary between sources (roughly 6100-5100 BCE, with some sources later).

research.lens: Childe's two 'revolutions' (Neolithic Revolution, 1936, and Urban Revolution, 1950, with its 10 criteria) and the later work that splits or reorders them: Bar-Yosef (Natufian sedentism), Zeder and Fuller/Asouti (domestication timeline, and whether it was protracted or rapid), Kuijt and Finlayson (storage before domestication), Bocquet-Appel (Neolithic Demographic Transition), Halstead (normal surplus), Flannery (household storage), Sherratt (Secondary Products Revolution), Kohler and Bogaard, Fochesato & Bowles (plough-linked wealth inequality), Johnson (scalar stress), Algaze (Uruk expansion) and Schmandt-Besserat (tokens to writing). Region: the Levant, Zagros and Mesopotamia. Main question: which of G1-G6 scholars treat as one transition, and where they draw the cuts.

periods_or_stages.name: Childe's 'Neolithic Revolution' (treated as one unit)
periods_or_stages.dates: Childe did not give fixed dates. In today's Near Eastern chronology his package runs from about 12,500 cal BC (Natufian) to about 6,500 cal BC (end of PPNB). He coined the term in Man Makes Himself (1936).
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Childe treated food production (crops and herds), settled villages, population growth and new crafts as one economic revolution, modelled on the Industrial Revolution. His package included pottery and weaving. In the Near East, pottery actually came about 2,500 years after cultivation began, in a phase archaeologists name 'Pre-Pottery Neolithic'.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G1 and G2 together. Childe would also have put the start of G3 crafts here, but the Near Eastern sequence separates them.
sources: Childe, V.G. 1936. Man Makes Himself. London: Watts. Summarised in Britannica: https://www.britannica.com/print/article/111108
Frieman, C. 2020. 'Revolutions so remote', Age of Revolutions: https://ageofrevolutions.com/2020/06/01/revolutions-so-remote-revolutionary-thinking-and-archaeological-inquiry/
Brami, M. 2019. Journal of World Prehistory, doi:10.1007/s10963-019-09135-y (on Childe's three revolutions)

periods_or_stages.name: Late Epipalaeolithic Natufian
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Stone-built houses, large settlements that were at least partly year-round, cemeteries and ornaments. Foragers harvested wild cereals but there was no domestication. Bar-Yosef calls it the 'threshold' to agriculture: villages came before farming.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G1 (村ができる). Sedentism separates out clearly as a stage before farming.
sources: Bar-Yosef, O. 1998. 'The Natufian culture in the Levant, threshold to the origins of agriculture.' Evolutionary Anthropology 6:159-177

Richter, T. et al. 2017. High-resolution AMS dates from Shubayqa 1 (Natufian ~14,600-11,500 cal BP): https://cris.biu.ac.il/en/publications/high-resolution-ams-dates-from-shubayqa-1-northeast-jordan-reveal/

periods_or_stages.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic A (PPNA)
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 11,700 to 10,700 cal BP (about 9,700 to 8,800 cal BC). The Paléorient literature places the PPNA/PPNB boundary around 8,800 cal BC in the north and later in the south.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Wild cereals were cultivated before they were domesticated. The Dhra' granaries (about 11,300 to 11,175 cal BP) are raised-floor stores built about 1,000 years before domestic cereals. Göbekli Tepe's monumental enclosures date to about 9,600 to 8,200 BCE. Zeder says humans were managing still-wild plants and animals by at least 11,500 cal BP.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Mainly late G1 / early G2. Stored surplus (a G3 idea) and communal ritual building already appear here.
sources: Kuijt, I. & Finlayson, B. 2009. PNAS doi:10.1073/pnas.0812764106. Summary: https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/06/090623150619.htm
Zeder, M. 2011. 'The Origins of Agriculture in the Near East.' Current Anthropology 52(S4):S221-S235: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/659307
Göbekli Tepe dating: Archaeology magazine 2021: https://archaeology.org/issues/may-june-2021/features/turkey-gobekli-tepe-hunter-gatherers/
PPNA/PPNB boundary debate, Paléorient: https://journals.openedition.org/paleorient/4076

periods_or_stages.name: Pre-Pottery Neolithic B (PPNB, Early to Late)
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 10,700 to about 8,500 cal BP (about 8,800 to 6,500 cal BC)
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Domesticated cereals: einkorn is abundant by about 10,400 cal BP. Goats were herded at Ganj Dareh about 10,000 cal BP; the evidence is culling of young males (Zeder & Hesse 2000). Round huts with shared storage give way to rectangular houses with private storage (Flannery 1972/2002). Late PPNB 'mega-sites' reach about 10-14 ha with 1,000 to 3,000+ people (Kadowaki; Rollefson). Kuijt links social crowding to the collapse of these big aggregated villages.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Core of G2 (畑と家畜). It also contains the first seeds of G4 (household-level storage and property) and G5 (scalar stress in large villages).
sources: Zeder, M. & Hesse, B. 2000. Science 287:2254-2257 (Ganj Dareh goats)

Flannery, K. 2002. 'The Origins of the Village Revisited: From Nuclear to Extended Households.' American Antiquity: https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-antiquity/article/abs/origins-of-the-village-revisited-from-nuclear-to-extended-households/5176075CEEFAE75EB9E8FEB1706ECCCE
Kuijt, I. 2000. Journal of Anthropological Archaeology 19:75-102, doi:10.1006/jaar.1999.0352: https://arheo.ffzg.unizg.hr/ska/tekstovi/people_space.pdf
Kadowaki 2012 (LPPNB mega-sites 10-14 ha): https://www.num.nagoya-u.ac.jp/outline/staff/kadowaki/laboratory/pdf/Kadowaki2012.pdf

periods_or_stages.name: Neolithic Demographic Transition (NDT), a process rather than a period
periods_or_stages.dates: Dated relative to the local start of farming, not in absolute years. In Europe and North Africa the share of juvenile skeletons rises 20-30% over about 500-700 years. The Levant is treated as the 'epicenter'. I could not verify Levant-specific absolute dates.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Cemetery data show an abrupt rise in the share of juvenile skeletons. Bocquet-Appel reads this as about +2 births per woman, caused by better maternal energy balance under farming. Fertility rises first and mortality rises later, the mirror image of the industrial demographic transition.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: The population engine of G1 and G2. It argues for treating 'more births' as a direct result of G2 farming rather than of G1 sedentism alone.
sources: Bocquet-Appel, J.-P. 2011. Science 333:560-561, doi:10.1126/science.1208880: https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00834316
Bocquet-Appel, J.-P. 2011. Current Anthropology 52(S4):S497-S510: https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/659243
Guerrero, Naji & Bocquet-Appel 2008. 'The Signal of the NDT in the Levant': https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00834967

periods_or_stages.name: PPNC / end-PPNB crisis
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 8,900 to 8,600 cal BP at Ain Ghazal (about 6,950 to 6,650 cal BC). Wider dislocation around the 8.2 ka event (about 6,200 BC) is debated.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Population at the mega-sites dropped sharply and southern Jordan was partly abandoned. Proposed causes are aridification, over-use of resources and social crowding. Big early villages did not lead straight to towns; they broke up into smaller ones.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: A failure mode at the G2/G3 boundary: G5-type problems (scale, disputes) appeared before there were leaders able to handle them.
sources: Zielhofer, C. et al. 2012. Quaternary Research (decline of Ain Ghazal): https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/journals/quaternary-research/article/decline-of-the-early-neolithic-population-center-of-ain-ghazal-and-corresponding-earthsurface-processes-jordan-rift-valley/A85EB4EEFBB2E10F9C11DD6161813B9E
Kuijt 2000 (as above)

periods_or_stages.name: Early Pottery Neolithic / Late Neolithic (Pre-Proto-Hassuna, Yarmukian, Çatalhöyük)
periods_or_stages.dates: Steady pottery production in Upper Mesopotamia from c. 7,000 to 6,700 cal BC. Coarse local ware c. 6,700 to 6,300 BC. Yarmukian in the Levant c. 6,400 to 6,000/5,900 BC. Çatalhöyük from about 7,400 to 7,100 BC to about 6,000 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: The first pots were rare and carefully made, and some were traded in rather than made locally. They later became a mass-produced craft at Tell Sabi Abyad. Milk fats in pots date to the 7th millennium BC (Evershed 2008). At Çatalhöyük each household kept 'private pantries' deep inside the house, while feasting displays (aurochs horns) eased the tension a full store created.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Start of G3 (余りと分業: part-time crafts, pottery) and early G4 (household storage). The first exchange of pots is an early, small seed of G6.
sources: Nieuwenhuyse, O. (ed.) 2018. Relentlessly Plain: Seventh Millennium Ceramics at Tell Sabi Abyad. Oxbow: https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/research/research-projects/archaeology/relentlessly-plain
Leiden paper on early ceramics: https://scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl/access/item%3A2863626/view
Yarmukian pottery: https://www.levantineceramics.org/wares/873-yarmukian-pottery
Evershed, R. et al. 2008. Nature 455:528-531: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18690215/

Bogaard, A. et al. 2009. 'Private pantries and celebrated surplus.' Antiquity 83:649-668: https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/journals/antiquity/article/private-pantries-and-celebrated-surplus-storing-and-sharing-food-at-neolithic-catalhoyuk-central-anatolia/3BAA8477B1B7E87B54D3D3EE79584327

periods_or_stages.name: Hassuna / Samarra / Halaf (northern and central Mesopotamia)
periods_or_stages.dates: Hassuna: early 6th millennium BC. Samarra: c. 5,500 to 4,800 BC (some put its start in the late 7th millennium). Halaf: c. 6,100 to 5,100 BC (Wikipedia); Nieuwenhuyse dates the rise of Halaf to c. 5,900 to 5,400 cal BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Painted fine wares made by craft specialists, early irrigation (Samarra), and widely shared styles. Frangipane contrasts 'horizontal' egalitarian Halaf with 'vertical' egalitarian Samarra/Ubaid, where privileged status sat alongside broad equality.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G3 together with the first stage of G4. It shows two different paths from 'surplus' to 'difference'.
sources: Frangipane, M. 2007. World Archaeology 39(2):151-176, doi:10.1080/00438240701249504: https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/93529
Halaf culture: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halaf_culture
Samarra culture: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samarra_culture

periods_or_stages.name: Ubaid period
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 6,500 to 3,800 BC (Wikipedia). The Met essay heading says 5,500 to 4,000 BC but gives an origin around 6,200 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Irrigation farming on the southern alluvium, tripartite houses, the first mud-brick public temples (Eridu) and stamp seals. 'Chieftain's houses' appear at Tell Abada and Değirmentepe. Stein (1994) describes small chiefdoms run on ritually mobilised 'staple finance' under an inclusive ideology. Burials show little sign of an elite. The culture spread north.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G5 (リーダーと決まり: leaders, dispute settlement) built on G4. The current G3 anchor 'Ubaid' fits G5 better, because pottery itself began about 500 to 1,000 years before Ubaid.
sources: Ubaid period: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubaid_period
Metropolitan Museum, 'The Ubaid Period' essay (2003): https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/the-ubaid-period-5500-4000-b-c
Belleten article on Ubaid elite households: https://www.belleten.gov.tr/tam-metin/61/eng
Stein, G. & Rothman, M. (eds.) 1994. Chiefdoms and Early States in the Near East. Prehistory Press

periods_or_stages.name: Sherratt's Secondary Products Revolution and the plough-and-land inequality step
periods_or_stages.dates: Sherratt (1981): 4th millennium BC in the Near East, early 3rd millennium BC in Europe. Bogaard et al.: ox-drawn ploughs about 6,000 years ago (about 4,000 BC) go with a doubling of household-wealth Gini. Counter-evidence: milk by the 7th millennium BC, and plough marks at Sion, Switzerland, in the early 5th millennium BC. Varna: 4,596-4,516 to 4,427-4,341 cal BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Animals came to be used for milk, wool, traction and transport, not only meat. Plough plus oxen made farming land-limited rather than labour-limited, so land became valuable and heritable. Kohler et al. (2017) show Old World Gini values (house sizes) kept rising after the Neolithic and tie this to large draft animals. Varna's gold-rich graves show a sharp early peak of inequality.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: A second, stronger stage of G4 (持ち物と差). Scholars separate it from the first stage (household storage, PPNB to 6th millennium) and put it late, at the end of the Chalcolithic, just before towns.
sources: Sherratt, A. 1981. 'Plough and pastoralism: aspects of the secondary products revolution.' In Hodder, Isaac & Hammond (eds.), Pattern of the Past. Overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_products_revolution

periods_or_stages.name: Late Chalcolithic / Early-Middle Uruk ('proto-urban' stage)
periods_or_stages.dates: Late Chalcolithic c. 4,500 to 3,100 BC overall. Tell Brak urban growth begins in the late 5th millennium BC (about 4,300 BC). Early Uruk c. 3,900 to 3,600 BC. Bullae and envelopes with complex tokens c. 3,700 to 3,500 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Tell Brak, a site of almost 300 ha, shows monumental building, industrial-scale production and high-status goods before writing and independently of the south (Oates et al. 2007). Susiana surveys show multi-level settlement hierarchies in the Early to Late Uruk phases (Johnson 1973; Wright & Johnson 1975). Mould-made, standard-size beveled-rim bowls appear; whether they were ration bowls is disputed. Sealed envelopes with tokens appear.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Transition from G5 to G6: towns and regional hierarchy come before writing, so 'town' and 'writing' should be separate milestones.

periods_or_stages.name: Late Uruk: Childe's 'Urban Revolution'
periods_or_stages.dates: c. 3,500 to 3,100 BC. Uruk IV / Eanna IVa tablets c. 3,350/3,300 to 3,200 BC. About 5,000 archaic tablets from Uruk date c. 3,300 to 2,900 BC. The network broke down around 3,000 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Uruk was perhaps the largest city in the world by about 3,200 BC: about 250 ha in the Met's figure (other sources say 80-100 ha), with up to 40,000-50,000 people by about 3,100 BC. Temple estates kept accounts of rations and herds. Colonies and outposts such as Habuba Kabira and Jebel Aruda were set up along trade routes (Algaze's 'Uruk World System'). Wool sheep, large-scale sculpture and full-time specialists appear. Childe's 10 criteria fit best here.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G6 (交易・町・記録). The state-like top level of G5 (fixed offices, 120 named officials) also arrives here.

periods_or_stages.name: Schmandt-Besserat's token-to-writing sequence
periods_or_stages.dates: Plain tokens from c. 8,000 or 7,500 BC; she argues for the earliest at Mureybet IIIb, c. 9,000-8,700 BC, alongside the first agriculture. Complex tokens in her 'Urban Period', 3,500 to 3,100 BC. Bullae and envelopes from about 3,700 to 3,500 BC. Numerical tablets in Uruk V, c. 3,500 to 3,350 BC. Proto-cuneiform c. 3,350/3,300 to 3,000 BC.
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Plain geometric tokens counted farm products. Incised complex tokens covered workshop goods. Tokens were sealed in envelopes, the envelopes were marked on the outside, those marks became numerical tablets, and finally pictographs were added. 88.5% of tokens in her sample came from sacred or public buildings.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: Spans G2 to G6. Simple tokens could start in G2/G3, complex tokens and bullae belong to late G5, and tablets and writing to G6.

periods_or_stages.name: Social-stage typology: Fried / Flannery & Marcus
periods_or_stages.dates: n/a
periods_or_stages.defining_features: Societies move from egalitarian, to achievement-based (prestige earned but not inherited), to hereditary rank (chiefdom; debts, genealogies, sacred lore manipulated), to kingdom or state. Flannery & Marcus argue that inequality comes from deliberate manipulation of social logic, not automatically from population growth or surplus.
periods_or_stages.maps_to_phases: G1-G2 egalitarian; G3-early G4 achievement-based; late G4-G5 hereditary rank; G6 state. This argues for splitting G4/G5 at the point where rank becomes inherited, not where wealth first differs.
sources: Flannery, K. & Marcus, J. 2012. The Creation of Inequality. Harvard University Press: https://prod.lsa.umich.edu/anthro/people/faculty/archaeological-faculty/kflanner/The-Creation-of-Inequality-How-Our-Prehistoric-Ancestors-Set-the-Stage-for-Monarchy-Slavery-and-Empir.html
